title: Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei)
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Scabies is a mite infestation causing intense pruritus and characteristic skin lesions. In low‑resource settings it often co‑exists with HIV, malnutrition, or eczema and may progress to crusted scabies.

sections.p: Scabies is a contagious ectoparasitosis caused by the human itch mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. It spreads by skin‑to‑skin contact and thrives in crowded, unhygienic environments common in many East African hospitals.
The adult female mite is ~0.3 mm, burrows into the stratum corneum, laying 2–3 eggs daily. Mites survive off‑host < 48 h, so transmission is mainly direct contact.
b: Life cycle: egg → larva (2 days) → nymph (5 days) → adult (10 days)
Mite burden: 10–15 in ordinary scabies, >10 000 in crusted scabies

sections.p: Skin‑to‑skin contact transmits mites; fomites (bedding, clothing) can spread crusted scabies. In immunocompromised hosts, unchecked replication leads to hyperinfestation.
b: Higher risk with HIV, steroids, malnutrition

sections.p: Two clinical forms exist: ordinary scabies with few mites and intense itch, and crusted (Norwegian) scabies with massive mite loads, thick crusts, and reduced itch.
b: Ordinary: 10–15 mites, burrows in wrists, interdigital spaces, waistline
Crusted: >10 000 mites, hyperkeratotic plaques, can act as a reservoir
Complications: secondary bacterial infection (Staph aureus, Streptococcus), post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis

sections.p: Clinical diagnosis is based on history and typical lesions; microscopy confirms by identifying mites, eggs, or feces from skin scrapings.

t.b: Does the patient have mites/eggs? Positive microscopy confirms scabies; negative does not exclude if clinical suspicion high.
Shows the ‘delta‑wing’ sign (mite head) and burrow tracks; useful when microscopy unavailable.
When labs unavailable, a typical distribution plus nocturnal itch in a contact‑case is sufficient to start treatment.

sections.p: First‑line topical scabicides are applied to the whole body; oral ivermectin is used for crusted scabies or when topical use is impractical.
b: Benzyl benzoate 25 % lotion – cheap, widely available; applied nightly for 3 days then repeat after 7 days.
Sulphur ointment 5–10 % – safe in infants and pregnant women; applied nightly for 3 days, repeat after 7 days.
Oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg – single dose, repeat after 7 days for crusted scabies; avoid in severe liver disease.

t.b: Prevents re‑infestation; all household members and close contacts receive the same regimen.
Wash bedding/clothing at 60 °C or seal in plastic for 72 h; essential for crusted scabies.
Empiric antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin) if cellulitis or impetigo present; reduces risk of renal complications.

sections.p: Focus on pattern of lesions, itch timing, and risk factors. Remember crusted scabies can be asymptomatic yet highly infectious.
b: Burrows in finger webs are pathognomonic.
Absence of itch in a severely immunocompromised patient suggests crusted scabies.
High mite load → need for ivermectin and strict isolation.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading erythema with fever (possible secondary sepsis)
Signs of acute kidney injury (hematuria, edema) after streptococcal infection

faq.q: Why does scabies itch more at night?
faq.a: Mite activity peaks in the dark and host cortisol levels fall, enhancing histamine‑mediated itch.

faq.q: Can scabies be transmitted by pets?
faq.a: Human scabies is caused by S. scabiei var. hominis; animal mites cause mange and do not sustain human infestation.

faq.q: Is it safe to use benzyl benzoate in infants?
faq.a: Yes, at 10 % concentration; avoid in newborns < 2 months, use sulphur ointment instead.

exam: A 4‑year‑old from a crowded orphanage presents with nocturnal itch and papules on wrists – what is your next step? — Perform a skin scraping; if unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical pattern.

A HIV‑positive adult with thick crusted plaques on elbows is diagnosed with crusted scabies – which two therapies are essential? — Oral ivermectin plus topical benzyl benzoate; also treat contacts and decontaminate environment.

A patient reports itching but skin exam is normal – which differential should you consider and why? — Early scabies may lack visible burrows; high suspicion warrants empirical treatment or dermatoscopy.
Why is sulphur ointment preferred in pregnancy over benzyl benzoate? — Sulphur has no systemic absorption and is classified as safe; benzyl benzoate carries teratogenic risk.

How does secondary bacterial infection complicate scabies and what is the management? — Staph/Strep can cause cellulitis or post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis; give appropriate antibiotics and monitor renal function.
In a resource‑limited clinic without microscopy, how would you confirm scabies? — Rely on classic distribution, nocturnal itch, and a history of contact; start treatment without lab confirmation.

What infection control measures are required for a patient with crusted scabies admitted to a ward? — Strict isolation, use of disposable gowns, wash all linens at high temperature, and treat all contacts.
Explain why ivermectin is contraindicated in severe liver disease. — Ivermectin is metabolised hepatically; impaired metabolism raises toxicity risk, so alternative topical therapy is chosen.
